guideTitle: 4 Best Leviton Motion Sensor Lights in 2026
metaTitle: Best Leviton Motion Sensor Lights in 2026
metaDescription: Four Leviton motion sensor light switches compared by amperage, wattage ratings, neutral wire needs and occupancy or vacancy mode for home rooms.
introParagraphs: Leviton makes motion sensor wall switches that swap in for the plain toggle on a bathroom, garage, laundry room or closet. The idea is old and sensible: walk in with full arms and the light is waiting, walk out and it shuts itself off. Many older homes have wallboxes with no neutral wire, which rules out a lot of smart switches, so a motion switch that does not demand one is a real find.

Only four of the listings in our research are true, distinct Leviton light switches, and we kept the list to those four rather than padding it. They differ in current rating, bulb wattage limits, circuit support and whether they turn the light on for you or leave that to your hand. We evaluated them on product specs and buyer feedback, concentrating on amperage, wattage ratings, wiring flexibility and room fit.
Because these go inside a wall, the sections after the picks spend time on the wiring checks that decide whether a switch is a good match before you buy.

products.name: Leviton 2A Motion Sensor Switch, No Neutral Required
products.description:
This is the most broadly useful Leviton in the lineup. It is a 2 amp motion switch that can run in auto-on and auto-off mode or in manual-on mode, giving households a choice about how the light behaves. The sensor offers a 180° field of view and 900 sq ft of coverage, which is generous for a bathroom, garage bay or laundry room. It can be installed with or without a neutral wire, though a ground is required.

Its load ratings are 150W for LED and CFL, 250W for incandescent and halogen, 200VA for magnetic low voltage and 250VA for electronic low voltage. That is plenty for a single fixture or a pair of bulbs, but it is not a switch for a large bank of lights. The slim profile is designed to fit in most wallboxes, which helps in older homes with cramped boxes.

Ownership is simple once it is wired, since the sensor does the work and the manual-on option lets you suit it to the room. Compared with the 5A model at 300W for LED and CFL, this one has half the LED load capacity, and compared with the 15A Decora it is far smaller. If you want a solid, flexible default for a typical room, this is where to start.

products.name: Leviton 5A Motion Sensor Switch, No Neutral Required
products.description:
The 5A Leviton uses the same 180° field of view and 900 sq ft coverage as the 2A model, but with a stronger electrical rating. It handles 300W of LED or CFL, 600W of incandescent or halogen, and 400VA of both magnetic and electronic low voltage lighting. Like the 2A, it runs in auto-on and auto-off or manual-on mode and does not require a neutral wire, though a ground is needed. The shallow design is meant to fit easily in the wallbox.

The higher rating matters for rooms with more than a couple of bulbs, such as a kitchen with several recessed cans or a long garage with multiple fixtures. At 300W for LED and CFL it carries twice the LED capacity of the 2A model. The tradeoff is that it is still a simple single-switch device, so it does not add dimming or fan control in its listing.

In practice it behaves exactly like the 2A, only with room to spare on the circuit. Against the 15A Decora it is far more modest at 5 amps, but it is also simpler and easier to fit in a tight box. Choose it when the 2A model's 150W LED ceiling worries you.

products.name: Leviton Decora Vacancy Motion Sensor Switch, DVS02-1LW
products.description:
This Decora DVS02-1LW is Leviton's vacancy model, meaning you switch the light on and the sensor switches it off when the room empties. It is a 2 amp single pole switch with a 180° field of view and 900 sq ft coverage. Its load ratings match the 2A occupancy model: 150W LED and CFL, 250W incandescent and halogen, 200VA magnetic low voltage and 250VA electronic low voltage. The slim profile fits most wallboxes, and it installs with or without a neutral, with ground required.

Manual-on has a clear advantage in shared bathrooms and bedrooms, since the light never surprises someone who is sleeping. It also saves a little energy because a light that only comes on when you choose is less likely to be triggered by a passerby. The drawback is the lost convenience of hands-free entry, which matters when you are carrying a load.

Ownership is easy to explain to a household: flip it on, forget it, and it turns off by itself. The hardware is the same size and rating as the 2A Auto model, so the choice is purely about behavior. If lights left burning is your issue more than lights failing to come on, this is the better fit.

products.name: Leviton Decora Occupancy Motion Sensor Switch, 15A
products.description:
The Decora Occupancy 15A is the heavy-duty option. It is a single pole switch that can also serve multi-way circuits, with the listing describing 3-way use with a DD0SR companion switch, or multi-sensor use with two DOS15 sensors where two sensors are needed. Its load ratings reach 600W for LED and CFL, 1800W for incandescent and halogen, and 1200VA for magnetic and electronic low voltage. It offers auto-on or manual-on operation, with the same 180° field of view and 900 sq ft coverage as the others.

That higher rating is useful for big rooms, workshops and garages with many fixtures. The multi-way capability helps in large spaces with two entrances. The tradeoff is that the listing does not state that this model works without a neutral, so wiring should be confirmed before purchase, and the companion devices add parts and planning.

It is the largest switch here and the one with the most flexibility, though it also asks the most from the buyer. Compared with the 5A model at 300W LED, it doubles the LED load to 600W. For anyone with a big room, multiple entrances or a heavy lighting load, it is the clear pick, while for a small closet it is far more than needed.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Many older homes have switch boxes with no neutral wire, and a switch that insists on one simply cannot be installed there. The Leviton 2A and 5A models and the Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW state that they install with or without a neutral, although a ground is required. The 15A Decora Occupancy listing does not say, so confirm before ordering. Open the wallbox with the breaker off and look for a bundle of white wires before you buy. If you find only a ground and the switched hot, favor the 2A, 5A or vacancy model.

Every switch has a limit, and LEDs, incandescents and low voltage lighting are rated differently. The 2A Leviton handles 150W of LED and CFL, the 5A handles 300W, and the 15A Decora Occupancy handles 600W. Add up the wattage of every bulb on the switch and leave a margin. A bathroom with a couple of 10W LEDs fits the 2A with no worry, while a garage with eight fixtures needs the 5A or 15A. A common mistake is assuming LED means low load on a circuit with many bulbs.

Occupancy switches turn lights on and off automatically, while vacancy switches leave turn-on to you. The 2A and 5A models can run in auto-on and auto-off or manual-on mode, the Decora Occupancy offers auto-on or manual-on, and the Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW is manual-on by design. Hands-free entry matters when you carry laundry or groceries. Manual-on matters in shared bedrooms and baths. Decide the behavior first, because it is the feature you will notice every day.

A motion switch sees only what it faces. The Leviton listings give a 180° field of view and 900 sq ft of coverage, which is wide for a wall-mounted unit. That suits a bathroom, laundry room or small garage. A room with an L-shape or large furniture may create blind spots the sensor cannot see. Think about where you stand when you stay still, such as at a sink or workbench, and be sure that spot is inside the 180° view.

A single pole switch controls a light from one place, while a multi-way setup needs companion devices. The 15A Decora Occupancy can work in 3-way with a DD0SR companion or with two DOS15 sensors for larger rooms, according to its listing. The 2A, 5A and vacancy models are described as single pole or do not mention multi-way support. If a hallway or large room has two entrances, plan the extra hardware before you buy. Skipping that step is how people end up with a switch that cannot be wired the way their house is built.

Motion switches are bulkier than toggles, and a crowded wallbox can make installation frustrating. The 2A and vacancy models are described as slim profile for most wallboxes, and the 5A is described as shallow. The 15A Decora handles more load and may need more room because of its capacity. Measure the box depth and count the wires inside before ordering. If the box is tight, the 5A shallow design or the slim 2A is the safer bet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wiring flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated how well each switch fits real wallboxes, especially older ones with no neutral. The 2A, 5A and vacancy models explicitly state they install with or without a neutral, while the 15A Decora does not make that claim. We counted that statement as a major advantage. Ground wire is required in all, which we flagged.

howWeEvaluated.title: Load capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared wattage ratings across LED, CFL, incandescent and low voltage loads. The 2A model carries 150W LED, the 5A carries 300W, and the 15A Decora carries 600W with 1800W of incandescent. A switch that cannot handle your load is unusable, so capacity carried real weight.

howWeEvaluated.title: Behavior options
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at whether a household can pick auto-on or manual-on. The 2A, 5A and 15A models support auto-on or manual-on, while the Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW is manual-on only. More options scored higher for general use, while the vacancy model was credited for its specific advantage in shared rooms.

howWeEvaluated.title: Coverage and sensing
howWeEvaluated.description: All four state a 180° field of view and 900 sq ft coverage, so sensing reach is a tie. We checked buyer feedback for complaints about lights shutting off while sitting still, which is a common issue with budget sensors. We did not credit any model with claims the listing did not make.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The 15A Decora Occupancy leads on capacity and multi-way support, the 5A leads on easy installation with moderate load, and the 2A leads on being the simplest all-round choice. The Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW leads for shared rooms where surprise light is a problem. No pick wins every category, so the badges reflect different jobs.

cards.label: Auto-on (occupancy)
cards.text: The light turns on by itself when it senses you and off after the room empties. The Leviton 2A, the 5A and the Decora Occupancy 15A support this mode, and each also offers manual-on. This is the best fit for garages, laundry rooms and kitchens where your hands are often full. Choose it when hands-free entry matters more than light control.

cards.label: Manual-on (vacancy)
cards.text: You switch the light on yourself, and the sensor turns it off when nobody is present. The Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW is built for this, and the 2A, 5A and 15A models can be set to it as well. It prevents lights from blazing on during a midnight visit or when someone walks past a doorway. Choose it for shared bathrooms and bedrooms.

howToChoose.note: If you are torn, the 2A model lets you try both behaviors without buying a different switch.

faq.q: How do I choose between the 2A, 5A and 15A Leviton switches?
faq.a: Add up the wattage of all the bulbs on the circuit. The 2A handles 150W of LED and CFL, the 5A handles 300W, and the 15A Decora handles 600W. A bathroom with a couple of LED bulbs is comfortable on the 2A, while a garage with many fixtures needs the 5A or 15A. Leave a margin below the rating rather than running right at the limit.

faq.q: Do these switches work without a neutral wire?
faq.a: The Leviton 2A, the 5A and the Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW state that they install with or without a neutral wire, though a ground wire is required. The 15A Decora Occupancy listing does not make that claim, so check before buying. Look inside the wallbox with the breaker off to see which wires are present. When in doubt, ask an electrician.

faq.q: What is the difference between occupancy and vacancy?
faq.a: An occupancy switch turns the light on and off automatically, while a vacancy switch leaves turning on to you. The Decora Vacancy DVS02-1LW is manual-on, and the other models offer auto-on or manual-on. Vacancy is calmer in shared bedrooms and baths. Occupancy is handier when your hands are full.

faq.q: Will the light turn off while I am sitting still?
faq.a: Any motion sensor can do this if you hold very still, which is a common complaint with budget models. The 180° field of view and 900 sq ft coverage help catch small movements across a room. If it happens, check that the sensor can see where you sit and that no furniture blocks it. A vacancy switch will not turn back on by itself.

faq.q: Can I use LED bulbs on these switches?
faq.a: Yes, the listings give LED and CFL ratings of 150W for the 2A and vacancy models, 300W for the 5A and 600W for the 15A. Stay under those numbers for the total of all bulbs on the switch. Very low-wattage LEDs can behave oddly on some switches, so test one bulb first if you are worried. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is installation a good DIY project?
faq.a: A basic swap of one switch is manageable for a comfortable DIYer who turns off the breaker and follows the instructions. Multi-way setups with the 15A model and its companions are more involved. A ground wire is required on all four. If you are unsure, hire a licensed electrician.

faq.q: Does the 180° view mean it covers the whole room?
faq.a: It means the sensor sees a wide half-circle in front of it, covering up to 900 sq ft according to the listings. Walls, doors and tall furniture can still create blind spots. Place the switch where it faces the room's main area, and think about where you stand still. In an L-shaped room, the far corner may need a second sensor.
